Bake for me — cloud lightmapping for live-lit scenes#

Verse streams best when a scene is baked: every surface carries its lighting in a texture, the engine draws it unlit, and what the visitor sees is exactly what the renderer in your DCC produced. Most archviz exports are baked (publish from Blender). Many are not — a model straight out of a configurator, a BIM export, a quick Blender scene with a few point lights — and those stream with Verse's live lighting, which is fast but not a render.

Bake for me closes that gap: pick it in the Lighting choice on the upload screen (or send one header) and the server traces the light through your scene into lightmaps before it compiles, so the link streams with the baked look.

On the upload screen#

Drop a GLB. The preflight shows a Lighting choice on every upload, in plain sight, with three options:

  • Keep as exported (the default): your file's materials and lights are shown live, exactly as they came out of your tool. You can relight the scene at any time with Make it look good or the Lights and Sun panels; nothing is baked.
  • Bake for me · preview: cloud lightmaps at 1K, a few minutes. A first look at the baked style.
  • Bake for me · final: 2K lightmaps, more samples, up to 20 minutes. For the published link.

When the file is live-lit (lights, no lightmaps) the app says so under the options; when it already carries baked lighting it says baking again is rarely needed. Pick a bake and upload: the build grows a Light stage (“Baking lighting · lightmap 12 of 40”), then carries on as usual. The finished link is the baked scene; the result says what the bake did (“Baked the lighting for you (preview quality): 40 lightmaps, 18.2 M texels in 6 min; 31 % of the surfaces can't be seen from where a visitor can walk and were left at a flat ambient level”).

The two bake qualities:

PresetLightmapsSamplesBudgetWhen
Previewup to 1024² per material, 24 M texels scene-wide32 per visible texel, up to 256 until the map is clean; 1 indirect bounce≤ 10 mina first look at the baked style, at a fraction of the time
Finalup to 2048², 96 M texels128 per visible texel, up to 1024 until clean; 2 bounces≤ 20 minthe hero link, once the model is settled

What preview means (2.7.2). A preview is a clean bake at a lower texel density, never a noisy one. Every lightmap is sampled until the preset's floor is reached and its grain (the median deviation of a texel from its neighbours on the same surface) is under 10 %, then an edge-aware denoiser takes the rest; a lightmap that is still grainy after that, or that no light reached, is not shipped — that material is shaded per vertex by the same tracer instead and the result says so. The app also tells you the samples per texel actually traced ("… 148 samples per texel, denoised").

Choose Keep as exported and the scene is published live-lit, exactly as it came out of your tool.

From the API and the SDK#

Code
curl -sS -X POST https://HOST/v1/ingest \
  -H "Content-Type: model/gltf-binary" -H "X-Verse-Name: flat-a" \
  -H "X-Verse-Bake: preview" --data-binary @flat-a.glb
Code
const { job } = await verse.upload(file, { name: "flat-a", bake: true });   // true = "preview"; or "final"
const rec = await verse.waitForJob(job);
console.log(rec.bake);  // { quality, seconds, texels, lightmaps, hiddenAreaFraction, … }

Resumable uploads pass bake in the begin body. While the job is in stage: "baking" the record carries live counters (bake.phase / done / total, workText); when it is done, the report — or bake.skipped with the reason the scene was compiled live-lit instead (see below). Full field list: docs/api.md § Bake for me.

What the bake does#

  1. Flattens the scene to world space and decides which materials can carry a bake: opaque, lit, not glass, not water or foliage (those keep their procedural lanes), not already a lightmap.
  2. Works out what a visitor can see. The compiler's occupancy grid gives the walkable floor; every triangle is shadow-ray tested from eye height over that floor. Surfaces nobody can reach a line of sight to — the back of a wardrobe, the top of a cupboard, the far side of exterior walls — are hidden: packed at half the texel density and never traced (they get a flat ambient level — half the median lit surface, never black). The report's hiddenAreaFraction says how much that was; on furnished interiors it is typically a third. Two-sided materials (doubleSided, which most archviz exports set on everything) are first turned to face open space: each triangle is probed from both sides and the side that sees the room wins, so a chair shell wound inside-out or a wall whose slivers point every which way bakes from the room's side, not from inside its own geometry (that was the black armchair).
  3. Charts and packs each material into one square lightmap, sized from its visible area and the preset's scene-wide texel budget.
  4. Traces: the glTF punctual lights (KHR_lights_punctual, point and spot; directional lights are not carried), emissive surfaces as area lights, and — when the file has no punctual lights at all — a sky and sun. An interior lit that way (an enclosed room with a window: the bake measures how much of the surface can see the sky) also gets an interior fill — the skylight a one-bounce tracer cannot carry around the room, credited to rays that travel a metre or two without hitting anything, so corners and under-furniture stay dark and open walls light up — instead of metering black and amplifying noise with a ×27 exposure gain (the production speckle). One or two indirect bounces. Progressive passes refine every lightmap to the preset's floor, then on while its grain is above 10 %, up to the ceiling or the wall-clock budget; big maps first.
  5. Finishes: a variance-guided, edge-aware denoiser (5 à-trous steps guided by each texel's world position, normal and running sample variance: grain is smoothed, contact shadows and sun edges are kept, charts never bleed), a quality gate (grain still above 6 %, or a map the light never reached → that material is shaded per vertex, not shipped as a lightmap), the material's own colour texture folded in, a metered exposure (the median visible surface lands at mid grey, highlights roll off softly, the gain capped at ×8), gutter dilation, PNG.

  6. Shades per vertex what a lightmap cannot carry: cut-out and blended materials (plant cards, decals — their holes live in the colour texture's own UVs, which a lightmap would replace), meshes finer than their lightmap (an 80 k-triangle armchair in a 256² map), and the lightmaps the gate refused. The same tracer lights every vertex (both sides of a two-sided surface, the brighter wins), the result goes into COLOR_0 and the material becomes KHR_materials_unlit with its texture and alpha mode intact. A live-lit material would shade black in a bake-dominant scene (there are no lights left in a fully-baked world), so this is what "kept live" means after a bake.

    One more black-plant cause lives in the file, not the bake: some exporters write a COLOR_0 vertex-colour layer of all zeros on meshes that never used one (the reception's plants and armchairs), and a vertex colour of black paints the mesh black on every path. The loader now drops an all-zero colour layer; a real vertex colour (any non-zero channel anywhere) is kept.

The output is an ordinary GLB whose baked materials are emissive-only (emissiveTexture + KHR_materials_emissive_strength) — the shape the compiler already recognises as a lightmap bake — so everything downstream (streaming, verification, versions, the classic fallback) is unchanged.

What it cannot do (yet)#

  • Animated or skinned scenes are not baked (a bake freezes lighting); they compile live-lit and the record says bake.skipped: "the scene is animated …". The same for scenes that are already baked.
  • Normal maps, roughness and metalness on baked materials are folded into flat diffuse lighting — a brushed-metal kitchen front bakes like a painted one. Keep such materials live by exporting them as glass or unlit, or bake in your DCC.
  • Charts are box projections, not an unwrap: a curved surface stretches a little across the seam between two projection directions, and a spiral stair can self-overlap. Walls, floors, furniture and anything built from flat faces are exact.
  • Units: glTF emissive has no physical unit; emissive 1.0 is taken as 100 cd/m² (VERSE_BAKE_EMISSIVE_NITS on the server). Exposure is relative, so only the balance between lamps and emissive panels is affected.
  • Two-sided surfaces are baked from the side that sees open space (probed per triangle); a thin wall seen from both sides gets one side's light on both.
  • Per-vertex shading (plants, refused maps, and the densest meshes) has no texel-level shadow detail: a leaf is lit as a whole. A dense mesh first gets a denser lightmap of its own (up to 4× the scene's texels per metre) and only falls back to per-vertex when even that cannot hold it.
  • Slatted surfaces box-project their slat sides into one-texel-high charts; they bake correctly but at the density of a texel per slat.

Operating it#

KnobEffect
VERSE_BAKE=0the stage is skipped on this server (the record says so)
VERSE_BAKE_TIMEOUT_Sthe bake's window (default 10 min preview, 20 min final); never more than leaves the compile half of the job clock. The compiler gets a deadline 8 % + 15 s inside it and always returns its best result before it; the window's end is only a backstop kill (then the scene compiles live-lit)
VERSE_BAKE_DEADLINE_S / --deadline-s(compiler) the whole bake's wall clock; the trace stops early enough for the finish to fit
VERSE_BAKE_GPU=0(compiler) never use the GPU tracer; by default it is used whenever an adapter is present (macOS builds always include it; Linux/Windows GPU boxes build with --features gpu)
VERSE_BAKE_THREADS(compiler) CPU threads for the bake (default: every core)
VERSE_BAKE_PARTS(server) force a fleet split into N parts; by default 1 + the bake-capable workers polling, at most 8
VERSE_BAKE_CACHE=0(compiler) trace every bounce exactly (no irradiance cache) — for references
VERSE_BAKE_DENSE_BOOST=0(compiler) dense meshes go straight to per-vertex shading (the 3.x behaviour)
VERSE_BAKE_BUDGET_S / VERSE_BAKE_TEXELSthe tracer's wall-clock budget when no deadline is given, and the texel budget (presets: 540 s / 24 M and 1800 s / 96 M)
VERSE_BAKE_EMISSIVE_NITSradiance of emissive 1.0 (default 100)
VERSE_BAKE_DENOISE=0skip the denoiser (for measuring what it removes)
VERSE_BAKE_GATE=0ship every lightmap, noisy or not, and keep dense meshes on lightmaps (inspection only)

Faster baking. The reference interiors bake final quality in minutes: a new BVH, one shared gather ray per sample, the sun traced once per texel, an irradiance cache for the bounce, and rounds that sample every lightmap evenly against a deadline. A Mac (or any GPU box running the worker) bakes on its GPU; fleet workers each bake a part of the lightmaps, so adding workers divides the time. verse-compile --bake-compare a.glb b.glb prints how different two bakes look (ΔE76 over the surfaces a visitor can see), independent of their lightmap layouts.

Locally: target/release/verse-compile --bake preview in.glb -o baked.glb prints the same progress: bake … lines the app shows and a bake-report: JSON line; cargo build --release -p verse-compile builds it.

Gates: node web/test/fix-verify-bake.mjs (ports 8780–8789) — the preflight detection, the compiler's output shape, the ingest stage and job record, both tiers' pixels (the wall near the lamp brighter than the far wall, no black walls, a floor gradient), and the un-baked ladder untouched; and node web/test/fix-verify-bake-quality.mjs (ports 8900–8909) — a sky-lit room with a window opening, a double-sided cut-out plant card and a dark-fabric sofa: clean wall and ceiling lightmaps on the shipped PNG, a lit plant, a non-black sofa, sppAchieved on the job record and the card, plus a real customer reception file as a skip-if-missing case (wall lightmap variance ≥ 5× lower than the un-denoised bake, the pair written to web/test/out/bake-quality/, plants and armchairs lit per vertex, preview under 3 min); and node web/test/fix-verify-fastbake.mjs (ports 9600–9649) — texel detail on a dense mesh against a 1024-spp reference, the deadline, byte-identical parts, the reference interiors' times (GPU, CPU, Railway-emulated) and ΔE76, distributed speedup with 1/2/4 parts, the fleet protocol with two workers and a tiny job clock.
